actions.justification: Mandatory: Patient has CKD stage 4 and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast. Hydration status assessment is critical for CI-AKI prevention planning.
Mandatory: Baseline eGFR is essential in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient to quantify renal risk prior to contrast exposure and guide prophylactic hydration and contrast volume decisions.
Mandatory: Patient has multiple risk factors for contrast-induced AKI (CKD stage 4, diabetes). Systematic risk factor review guides pre-procedural mitigation strategy.
Establish current hemodynamic baseline before procedure; hemodynamic instability increases risk of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk CKD stage 4 + diabetes patient.
Review medications for nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, metformin) that should be held before contrast administration in this CKD stage 4 patient to reduce AKI risk.
Calculating maximum safe contrast volume (e.g., 3-5x eGFR formula) is a key preventive step for CIN in this high-risk patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes — both are major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Before proceeding with contrast-based cardiac catheterization, alternative imaging modalities should be considered to minimize contrast exposure risk.

CKD stage 4 with diabetes significantly elevates risk for acute kidney injury post-contrast. Nephrology consultation is indicated to guide peri-procedural management, optimal hydration strategy, and post-procedure monitoring.

Prior to cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure, all nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.) should be identified and held to minimize additive renal injury risk in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is planned for cardiac catheterization with contrast. Documenting the eGFR check is essential to establish baseline kidney function and risk-stratify for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prior to the procedure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Discontinuing nephrotoxic agents (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin) before contrast administration reduces risk of acute kidney injury.
Monitoring urine output in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient prior to catheterization helps assess hydration status and baseline renal perfusion, guiding pre-procedural IV fluid administration.

Pre-procedural IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid (normal saline) is the cornerstone of CIN prevention in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 undergoing contrast-enhanced cardiac catheterization. Volume expansion protects the kidneys by diluting contrast and maintaining renal perfusion.

Metformin should be held peri-procedurally in diabetic patients with CKD (eGFR <60) receiving iodinated contrast due to risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury leading to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis. This patient has both diabetes and CKD stage 4.

Post-procedure serum creatinine at 48 hours is recommended to detect contrast-induced nephropathy, which typically peaks 48-72h after contrast exposure. Planning this now ensures follow-up monitoring is in place before the procedure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned cardiac catheterization (contrast exposure). Holding nephrotoxic medications is critical to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient.

Patient with CKD stage 4 (eGFR likely <45) and diabetes should have metformin held peri-procedure as contrast administration with metformin risks lactic acidosis, especially in advanced CKD (G3b or worse).
Pre-planned IV hydration post-contrast is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes). Isotonic crystalloid hydration reduces contrast nephropathy risk.

CKD stage 4 patient undergoing cardiac catheterization with contrast. Pre-procedure IV hydration (isotonic saline) is a cornerstone of contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients. This has not yet been completed per the already-done list.

Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient to assess hydration status, renal perfusion, and early signs of acute kidney injury prior to and following contrast administration.

Post-contrast serum creatinine monitoring at 48-72 hours is required to detect contrast-induced nephropathy in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Planning this now ensures follow-up is not missed.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Serial creatinine monitoring at 72 hours post-contrast is essential to detect delayed AKI, as SCR at 48h has already been checked.

Patient with CKD stage 4 (severely reduced GFR) and diabetes undergoing contrast procedure warrants nephrology input to guide ongoing management, assess need for renal replacement therapy, and optimize post-procedure renal protection strategies.
